activity: to compare simple and compound interest on a savings account over five years
knowledge_domain: to compare simple and compound interest on a savings account over five years
fact: Simple interest is paid only on the original amount deposited, called the principal, so it adds the same dollar amount every year.
story:
Mackenzie had one goal at the mall: convince her dad that a phone upgrade made sense before eighth grade started. She had her argument ready, complete with a coherent list of reasons she'd rehearsed in the car. But on the way to the phone store, they passed a bank kiosk with a banner that said TEEN SAVINGS, START TODAY, and her little sister Priya stopped dead.

"I want to open one," Priya announced. "Alyssa's in that category, kids with accounts, and she says they're basically rich."

"They're not rich," Mackenzie said, but she was already eyeing the display table, where a sample statement lay pinned under plastic. The table had a five-year plan sheet, and a rep was inviting anyone who wanted to participate in a quick demonstration. Mackenzie raised her hand before her dad could steer them onward.

The rep slid over a mock statement for something called simple interest. Mackenzie scanned the column of yearly interest payments and frowned. "Wait. This is wrong, isn't it? Year one is twelve dollars, year two is twelve dollars, all five years are twelve dollars. Shouldn't it grow?"

"That's what simple interest does," the rep said. "It's paid only on the original deposit."

"That's called the principal," Priya read off the sheet, tapping the word with her finger. "The original amount deposited."

Mackenzie grabbed the second sheet, the one marked compound, and laid them side by side. "Okay, so on this one, year one is twelve dollars, but year two is more. Twelve dollars and something." She checked the third year, then the fourth. "It keeps climbing. So the simple one adds the same dollar amount every single year, like a flat staircase, and this one is more like a ramp." She pulled out her phone and totaled both columns. Simple interest gave sixty dollars over five years. Compound gave more, and the gap widened every year.

"I changed my mind about the phone," she said suddenly. "Sort of. If I put my four hundred dollars of birthday money in the compound one instead, by the time I actually need a new phone, the interest does part of the work for me." Her dad raised an eyebrow, and she held up the sheet like evidence. "Look at year five. It's not a huge difference, but it's free."

"Can I get one too?" Priya asked. "I have thirty-one dollars."

"You can get anything you want with thirty-one dollars," the rep said, laughing, and slid a starter form across the table.

Priya snatched the pen and started printing her name, letter by careful letter, while Mackenzie filled in her own form and circled the word compound at the top twice, hard enough to dent the page.

activity: to improvise a scene with a partner by accepting each offer with yes, and
knowledge_domain: to improvise a scene with a partner by accepting each offer with yes, and
fact: Endowing means giving your partner a role or trait through what you say, as in 'Doctor, my arm hurts', which makes them the doctor.
story:
Sebastian's sister Priya stood in the middle of the living room with her arms crossed, staring at the carpet like it owed her money. "I froze again," she said. "Third time today. Monday I have to improvise a scene in front of the whole drama class, with a partner I've never even met."

"You? Freeze?" Sebastian set down his book. Priya performed constantly, narrating their mom's cooking like a nature documentary, dramatizing every scraped knee. Freezing made no sense, so something hidden had to be causing it. He needed to see it happen.

"Okay, do one with me. I'll be your partner."

"Fine. You start something and I'll join in." She cleared her throat and shook out her hands.

Sebastian had no idea what improv partners actually did, so he just said, "Hi, I need help." Priya opened her mouth, then closed it. Her eyes darted around like she was searching for the right answer and finding none.

"See?" she whispered.

He chewed on that. The problem wasn't her imagination, because she had plenty. The problem was that "I need help" gave her nothing to be. What if the first line had to nominate a role for the other person, the way a costume did? He tried again, changing one thing.

"Doctor, my arm hurts," he said, holding his elbow. "You're the only one at this clinic."

Priya snapped upright. "Sit down, sit down, this looks serious. Nurse, bring the x-rays!" She was suddenly brisk and bossy, stethoscope made of a jump rope, and for two whole minutes they ran a hospital where Sebastian's arm had been crushed by a falling turbine blade, which he invented on the spot, and Priya declared the clinic "impoverished, with no anesthesia but plenty of spirit." They were both laughing by the end.

"It's like you handed me a costume," Priya said, catching her breath. "At drama camp they called it endowing. Giving your partner a role through what you say. I forgot."

"So Monday, if your partner just stands there being vague, you fix it."

"By endowing them first. 'Captain, we've cleared the asteroid field.'" She spun in a circle, pretending to dodge asteroids. "Or, 'Professor, the volcano's about to blow.'" Then she stopped and pointed at him. "You're my brother and also my hero. Now hold still, Doctor, this turbine accident won't survive without you."

activity: to draw a street using one-point perspective with lines meeting at a vanishing point
knowledge_domain: to draw a street using one-point perspective with lines meeting at a vanishing point
fact: Masaccio's Holy Trinity fresco in Florence, painted around 1427, is one of the earliest paintings built on a single vanishing point.
story:
Cameron wanted his street to look real, the way the one in his head did, with buildings leaning in like they were listening to each other. Instead his drawing looked flat, like buildings pasted onto cardboard. Ms. Ruiz had pinned a print of an old fresco above the supply shelf, and Cameron kept glancing at it while his pencil stalled.

A girl about his age, Dana, was standing in front of the print with her finger hovering over the glass. "Watch," she said. "The ceiling lines, the floor lines, they all run to one spot." She dragged her finger along each edge of the painted vault, and every one, ceiling and floor and side arches, aimed at the same small point directly beneath the cross. "It's Masaccio's Holy Trinity, from Florence," she said. "Painted around 1427. My aunt says it's one of the earliest paintings built on a single vanishing point."

"A vanishing point," Cameron repeated. The words felt like a spell name. He looked back at his flat street and devised a plan on the spot: he would become a scavenger of lines, hunting every edge in his drawing the way Dana had hunted the fresco's, and dragging them all to one mark.

He started with a hypothetical street where he already knew the answer, one straight road, two rows of buildings, one point dead ahead. He tapped a dot in the center of the page, then drew a roofline from the top corner of a building straight to the dot. It looked wrong until he added the ground line slanting to the same spot, and suddenly the building leaned back in space like it had weight and a shadow. The road itself was just two lines running together, but now it ran somewhere.

"Every edge obeys the dot," Cameron said, half to Dana, half to his pencil. He imagined the dot as a tiny magnet buried in the road, pulling every brick and windowsill toward it, and him too, if he stood on the paper. Windowsills slanted up toward it from below; roofs slanted down to it from above. The street began to breathe.

He drew a lamppost near the front and made it tall, then a matching one far down the street, small, its top aimed at the same invisible mark. Dana leaned over his shoulder. "It's like standing inside it," she said. Cameron put his finger at the vanishing point and pressed down, like he was holding the whole street in place.

activity: to explain how a river carves a canyon over millions of years through erosion and deposition
knowledge_domain: to explain how a river carves a canyon over millions of years through erosion and deposition
fact: A delta forms where a river slows as it enters a sea or lake and drops the sediment it was carrying, building up new land.
story:
Nathaniel stared at the assignment sheet on the kitchen table. "Explain how a river carves a canyon over millions of years," he read aloud. "Presentation Thursday." His problem was simple and enormous: how could he show something that took millions of years when he had four days? He couldn't exactly demolish the backyard with a river. He needed a way to make time itself smaller.

His little sister Priya wandered in, eating toast. "What's a canyon doing on your homework?" she asked. He told her, and she shrugged. "You need a river, obviously." That gave him an idea. He grabbed the garden hose, a plastic bin, and the big bag of play sand from the garage, and dumped it all on the patio in a sloping pile. If a real river could carve rock over millions of years, maybe a trickle of water could carve sand in an afternoon. It was worth testing.

He packed the sand into a smooth slope, dug a small pond at the bottom and filled it with water, then turned the hose to a trickle at the top. At first nothing happened except dark wet patches spreading. Then the water found a path and began to run, and within minutes it had cut a channel as deep as his thumb. He cheered so loudly that Priya came back out. When the channel collapsed and the flow split into two directions, he faced a dilemma: dam one side, or let the river choose? Priya voted to let it choose. "Be impartial," she said. "It's your river's decision."

So he let it run, and something strange happened where the water reached the pond. The current slowed, and all the sand it had been carrying sank right there, building a spreading fan of new land that pushed out into the water like a small triangle. Nathaniel crouched at the pond's edge. Every grain the river had torn from the slope upstream was being dropped downstream, and the fan kept growing, grain by grain. "I've seen a picture of this," he said slowly. "It's called a delta." Priya leaned over and patted the wet little triangle. "Ours is better than the picture."

Thursday came, and Nathaniel carried the whole bin to school with a spray bottle to keep the river alive. During his presentation, he ran the water and let his classmates watch the delta grow while he described the canyon millions of years wide and the river patient enough to carve it. When it was over, Priya was waiting at the classroom door, since Mom had brought her along. "So?" she asked. "Did our river behave?"

Nathaniel held up the bin, delta still dripping. "It built land out of nothing," he said. "Want to see it do it twice?"

activity: to chop an onion safely with the claw grip and make a pasta sauce from scratch
knowledge_domain: to chop an onion safely with the claw grip and make a pasta sauce from scratch
fact: A damp cloth or damp paper towel under a cutting board stops the board from sliding across the counter while you chop.
story:
Sydney pressed the knife down and the cutting board shot sideways like a hockey puck, carrying the half-chopped onion with it. "Whoa," said Marcus, the young cook running the pasta sauce demo at the farmers' market. "Board's got a mind of its own today."

Sydney retrieved the onion from where it had rolled under the table of tropical fruit, between a papaya and a pineapple. She had signed up for this demo because her grandmother had made sauce from scratch every Sunday, and Sydney wanted to cherish that tradition by learning it herself. So far she had learned that raw onions made her cry, and that a cutting board with wheels was a real hazard.

She stared at the board. It had slid twice now, both times right when she pushed down with the knife. Was it the counter? The counter was smooth and a little damp from a spilled sample of peach juice. Wait. Damp. Something tickled the back of her mind.

Last summer at her friend Priya's house, the same thing had happened. Priya's board skidded every single time she pressed down, and they had chased diced peppers all over the kitchen like scavengers hunting crumbs. Then Priya's older brother had wandered in, folded a paper towel, run it under the tap, and slid it under the board before vanishing with a whole sleeve of crackers. After that, the board had sat still as a stone. Sydney had never wondered why. Now she did.

"Can I try something?" she asked Marcus. He raised an eyebrow but nodded. She folded a paper towel, soaked it at the water jug, wrung it out, and laid it flat on the counter. Then she set the board on top. She curled her fingers into the claw grip Marcus had shown her, knuckles forward like a tiny armor, fingertips tucked safely back, and cut into the onion. The board did not move. She pressed harder. Still nothing. It sat there as if glued. Sydney grinned so wide she nearly lost her claw grip.

"Okay, what did you just do?" Marcus asked, leaning over the counter.

"A damp paper towel under the board," Sydney said. "My friend's brother did it once. I didn't know it worked until right now."

"Huh. I've been meaning to buy the rubber mats with grip bumps," Marcus said, "and instead the answer was a towel and some water."

"Want to know the weird part? I have no idea why it works. It just does."

"Those are my favorite kinds of answers," Marcus said. He slid a heavy pot onto the burner and nodded at her onion, now chopped into neat little pieces. "Now let's make it something your grandmother would be proud of. Oil first, and remember, the garlic goes in for thirty seconds only, or we'll all be tasting burnt bits until December."

Sydney picked up the knife again.

activity: to chop an onion safely with the claw grip and make a pasta sauce from scratch
knowledge_domain: to chop an onion safely with the claw grip and make a pasta sauce from scratch
fact: Simmering a sauce with the lid off lets water escape as steam, so the sauce slowly gets thicker.
story:
Eve had wanted to work in her family's restaurant kitchen since she was eight, which was why it stung that her first real Saturday shift began with forty pounds of onions. Her uncle Nick handed her a knife and said, "Claw grip. Fingers curled, knuckles forward, so the blade rides along them instead of your fingertips."

"Like this?" Eve bent her fingers under and the knife bumped her knuckles, harmlessly, like a boat nudging a dock.

"Exactly. It looks timid, but timid keeps your fingers." He walked off toward the fryer, and she began to chop, slowly at first, then faster, until there was a mountain of little white cubes and only the faint stinging that her grandmother claimed meant the onion was fresh, a claim Eve privately suspected had nothing to do with anything.

Her grandmother put her on the pasta sauce next, which felt like a promotion. "Tomatoes, the onion, garlic, salt. Cook it. I'm doing tables." Then she was gone, and Eve was alone with a pot and a stove, which coincided nicely with her secret plan: if the sauce was good, she'd get assigned to it every Saturday, and Saturdays in the kitchen were the best place in the building.

She dumped everything in, brought it to a boil, and set the lid on tight because that seemed like the careful, responsible thing to do. Then she went back to chopping more onions, feeling extremely professional.

An hour later her grandmother swept past, lifted the lid, and frowned. "It's thin," she said, tilting the spoon so the sauce ran off it fast, like juice.

"I followed the recipe exactly," Eve said. "Every measurement."

Her grandmother stirred, tasted, and looked at the pot instead of Eve, which somehow made it worse. "It's a half hour before the dinner rush, and I need this thick."

Eve stood there, staring at the lid in her hands. The sauce had been bubbling the whole time. Bubbling meant steam, and steam was water, and the lid was right there, trapping it, sending it back down as drips along the rim. The pot was a sealed box with nowhere for the water to go. She thought about the puddle of sauce on the counter, thin as it was, and about how steam fogged a bathroom mirror when the door stayed shut.

She lifted the lid off completely and set it on the counter. "Leave it off," she said, half to herself. "The steam gets out, and the sauce gets thicker." It was a guess, but a satisfying one, and she watched the surface bubble open to the air.

Twenty minutes later, the spoon stood up in the pot for a second before slowly tipping over. Her grandmother dipped bread in it, chewed, and said nothing, which in her grandmother's language was applause.

"Next Saturday," her grandmother said, "you're on sauce again. Lid stays off."

"The lid and I had a disagreement," Eve said. "I won."

activity: to change a flat bicycle tyre using tyre levers and a pump
knowledge_domain: to change a flat bicycle tyre using tyre levers and a pump
fact: A Presta valve has a small nut on top that must be unscrewed before any air can be pumped in or let out.
story:
Mila leaned her bike against the railing outside the First Provincial Bank and saw the problem right away: the back tyre was flat as a ribbon. She had ridden here to deposit her birthday money before the branch closed at noon, and now the wheel would not roll another block.

She opened her backpack and found the note her neighbor Renata had slipped under her door that morning. "Take the repair kit I left in your saddlebag," it read. "Tyre levers, patch, pump. Unscrew nothing until you know what it is. Call me if the pump fights you. Renata." Mila read it twice, then flipped the bike upside down on the bank's wide stone steps.

A bee worked the nectar out of the petunias in the flowerbed beside her while she wedged the first tyre lever under the tyre's edge. The lever snapped in, and she worked a second one around the rim, peeling the tyre back until the inner tube came loose. She found the leak by pumping a little air in and holding the tube against her wet forearm. A thin stream of bubbles rose off one spot. She applied the patch from Renata's kit, pressed it flat, and tucked the tube back inside the tyre.

Then she pumped. Ten strokes, twenty, thirty, and the tyre stayed soft. She squeezed it, pumped harder, and got nothing. She sat back on the steps and looked at the valve, the little metal stem sticking out through the rim. On top of it sat a small nut, screwed down tight. Renata's note said to call if the pump fought her, but first Mila tried to interpret it her own way. The note warned her about unscrewing things she didn't understand, yet the pump and the tube were connected only through this valve, and nothing else between them could stop the air.

She pinched the small nut and turned it counterclockwise until it wobbled loose. She pressed the pump head on again and gave one stroke. The tyre firmed up under her hand. She pumped until it was hard, then unscrewed the pump and screwed the little nut back down snug. When she let out a breath, a steady hiss came from nowhere, and she checked the valve, pressing it gently with her thumbnail until the hiss stopped.

Inside, the teller counted her bills. "Fix that yourself?" the woman asked, stamping the deposit slip. "Diligent kid."

"Somebody left me a note," Mila said. "But the nut was my own find."

activity: to write a short story with correctly punctuated dialogue and a clear climax
knowledge_domain: to write a short story with correctly punctuated dialogue and a clear climax
fact: When a dialogue tag interrupts one spoken sentence, the second part of the quote begins with a lowercase letter because the sentence is continuing.
story:
Jeremy slid his draft across the kitchen table, and Mom picked it up while the spaghetti water churned behind her, steam fogging the window over the sink. The story was due tomorrow, and he had a problem bigger than the leaky plumbing under the bathroom sink, which was saying something, because Dad had been under there all weekend with a wrench.

"Read this part out loud," Mom said, tapping the page. "Where your hero meets the robot."

Jeremy read. "'I know your secret,' the robot said. 'And I will tell everyone at the science fair.'" He stopped. Something felt wrong, like a random note stuck in the middle of a song, but he couldn't point to why.

"Is that one thing the robot says, or two?" Mom asked.

"One thing. It's all one speech." Jeremy frowned at the paper. Then he grabbed a pencil and drew a big curved arrow from the first quote, looping under the words "the robot said," and landing on the second quote. "It's one sentence. The tag is just... interrupting it. Like my math teacher walking between our desks during a test. The sentence keeps going on the other side."

"So what should the second part look like?"

Jeremy stared. Capital A. Lowercase a. He said both versions out loud, tapping the table on each word. "And I will tell everyone" started sounding like a continuation, not a new start. He erased the capital A and wrote a lowercase a, then changed the period after "said" to a comma. "There. It's still one sentence, so the second part starts small."

"Now read it again," Mom said, draining the spaghetti so the steam rolled up in a hot white cloud.

"'I know your secret,' the robot said, 'and I will tell everyone at the science fair.'" Jeremy grinned so wide his cheeks hurt. It flowed now, like water through a clear pipe instead of spraying every which way.

Then he froze. "Wait. My climax. The robot's big reveal has the same thing. Three times." He flipped the page and found the moment where the robot points at the villain in front of the whole school. He fixed all three lines, hand flying, pencil squeaking, while Mom set two plates of spaghetti down and the rich smell of garlic filled the kitchen.

"Done," Jeremy announced, holding the page up like a trophy. "Fixed the dialogue and the climax lands right at the reveal. Mrs. Okafor is going to think a professional wrote this."

Mom sat down and twirled her fork. "Read me the ending," she said.

activity: to recognise signs of stress and use deep breathing and sleep routines to manage it
knowledge_domain: to recognise signs of stress and use deep breathing and sleep routines to manage it
fact: Box breathing means breathing in for a count of four, holding for four, breathing out for four and holding for four, then repeating the pattern.
story:
Evan sat in the waiting room with his hands pressed flat on his knees, because last time he had chewed his thumbnail down to the quick before his name was even called. He was here for his flu vaccine, which he honestly did not mind. What he minded was the paper he was clutching, the one from school saying he had to give a speech in front of his whole class on Friday. His stomach had been hurting since Tuesday, and he had started wondering if the two things were parallel, running side by side, or if one was actually causing the other.

When Dr. Okafor came in, she asked the usual questions, then paused. "Stomachaches, trouble sleeping, and you say your hands go cold before tests? Any fever?" No fever, Evan admitted. He had even tried to isolate the problem, skipping breakfast one morning to see if food was the cause, but the ache had shown up anyway. His best friend's sister had a poster in her room, he remembered now, a square drawn on it with the words "Box breathing" underneath, and she had traced it with her finger while studying. At the time he'd thought it was weird, something girls did, and he had changed the subject. Now he was less sure he'd been right to laugh it off.

"Can I ask you something?" Evan said. "My friend's sister traces a square when she's stressed. Does that actually do anything?"

Dr. Okafor nodded and pulled a blank sheet from her printer. She drew a square, nothing else, and slid it across. "It's called box breathing," she said, and that was all.

Evan studied the shape. In for four, he guessed, moving up one side. Hold for four along the top. Out for four going down, then four more along the bottom, and around again. He traced it slowly, breathing with his finger, and by the third lap his shoulders had dropped somewhere lower. His stomach did not vanish, but it went quiet, like a radio turned down.

"Friday," he said. "I could do this at my desk before the speech." He was already planning it: trace the square on the desk where nobody could see, four counts each side, and in bed that night he would try it too, lights off at nine instead of lying awake till eleven with his phone.

Dr. Okafor held up the syringe for his vaccine and smiled. "Ready?"

Evan put out his arm, traced one small square on his knee with his free hand, and said, "Four, four, four, four. Go ahead."

activity: to read the periodic table and find the number of protons in an element from its atomic number
knowledge_domain: to read the periodic table and find the number of protons in an element from its atomic number
fact: The periodic table arranges the elements in order of increasing atomic number, so each element has one more proton than the element before it.
story:
Carson's science fair project was supposed to be about microbes in pond water, but the judge was stopping at his table in four minutes, and his poster still had a blank square where the element key should go. He had taped a periodic table chart next to his microscope, because the stain he'd found would only make sense if he could say what the mineral in the water was. The problem was, he had never actually learned to read the chart.

Last summer flashed back to him: his grandfather pointing at a faded periodic table in the garage and saying, "Numbers, boy. Everything on that table answers to numbers." Carson had nodded and then gone inside to eat a popsicle. Now he wished he'd stayed and listened.

His friend Priya slid over from the next table, holding her invasive-plant display like a shield. "Judge's on table six. You look like your microbe died."

"Worse. I have to identify the element in my sample, and this chart is just a wall of squares." He ran his finger across the top row. "Hydrogen, one. Helium, two. Lithium, three."

"Wait," Priya said. "Look at the numbers in the corners. One, two, three, four. They count up by one, all the way across."

Carson followed the little numbers down the chart. Carbon, six. Nitrogen, seven. Oxygen, eight. Every single square, one more than the one before it. "So the table goes in order," he said slowly. "Increasing atomic number, all the way through."

"That's why it's called the periodic table and not the random table," Priya said.

He grabbed the printed results from his water test. His sample showed an element with seven protons. Seven. He traced the numbers again, six, seven, and his finger landed on nitrogen. Then the twist hit him: his pond water sample had nitrogen in it, which meant something was dumping fertilizer upstream, which meant his microbes weren't just interesting, they were evidence. He wrote "7 protons = nitrogen" in the blank square just as the judge's badge appeared at the edge of his table.

"Tell me about your project," the judge said.

Carson took a breath and began, "I'll narrate it from the pond, if that's okay. It starts with water, a microscope, and a chart I didn't understand until ten minutes ago." Priya, behind the judge, gave him two thumbs up.

activity: to use a primary source like a settler's diary to explain why people moved west in the 1800s
knowledge_domain: to use a primary source like a settler's diary to explain why people moved west in the 1800s
fact: A settler's diary shows one person's view; it rarely tells how the Native American nations whose lands the trails crossed saw the same events.
story:
Grayson spread the old diary across his grandmother's kitchen table, careful of the cracked leather cover. His history teacher had assigned each student a primary source, an actual document from the 1800s, and Grayson had been smug when his grandmother mentioned the diary of a settler named Harriet Cole that had been in the family for generations. A primary source nobody else in the class could touch. He might even win the prestigious county history prize with it, if his report was good enough.

He read aloud while his grandmother dried dishes. "March the fourteenth. We have taken the trail at last. Ezekiel says the land beyond the river is free for the taking, and our crop failed twice in Ohio, so what choice have we?" Grayson copied the line onto his notecard. "This is perfect. It explains why they moved. Farm failure, and land." He wrote a heading: Why People Moved West.

But then he slowed down. Free for the taking, Harriet had written. Grayson looked at the window, where rain was beginning to dissolve the last snow of the year into gray streaks on the glass. The trails crossed land, he thought. Land that was already somewhere, already somebody's. Harriet's diary was one person's view of the journey. It never once said how the Native American nations whose lands the trails crossed saw those same events. He flipped through page after page. Wagons stuck in mud, a fever, a birth, a river crossing. Nothing at all from the other side.

He decided to test a simple idea. "Grandma, did anyone in the family ever write down the other view? Anything?" He figured the answer would be no, and that the consequence would be a report missing half its story, a coin with only one face. His grandmother set down her towel, went to the sideboard, and came back with a folder.

"Twist for you," she said. "This belonged to my mother, and she got it from her mother." Inside was a typed page, an oral history recorded in the 1930s, of an old woman remembering her grandmother's account of wagons coming through her people's hunting grounds one season after another. The woman described watching the grass change, watching strangers measure the ground with chains.

Grayson read it twice. Then he wrote a new heading under the first one: What Harriet Could Not See. His two sources sat side by side on the table, the leather diary and the typed page, and for the first time his report had both banks of the river in it.

"Now that," his grandmother said, tapping the folder, "is a story with a whole horizon."

activity: to improvise a scene with a partner by accepting each offer with yes, and
knowledge_domain: to improvise a scene with a partner by accepting each offer with yes, and
fact: In improv, an offer is anything a performer says or does that gives information about the scene, such as a place, a name or a problem.
story:
Sofia dragged the kitchen chairs to the middle of the living room and set them facing each other, two feet apart. In three days she had to improvise a scene with a partner in front of the whole drama club, and the only rule Mrs. Okafor had written on the board was "yes, and." Sofia did not know what the "and" part was supposed to add.

Her older brother Marcus wandered in with a granola bar. "What's with the chairs?"

"Practice with me. We have to make up a scene together, and I keep freezing." She sat down. "Just start something. Anything."

Marcus plopped into the other chair, stretched out his arms like he was holding a long pole, and pretended to reel something in. Sofia stared at him. Was he tired? Reaching for something? She said, "Are you okay? You look weird."

"That's not it." He dropped his arms. "I'm fishing. I was setting up a scene on a boat. You could've said I was hauling in a shark or something."

Sofia sat up straight. So the way he held his arms was doing a job. It told her where they were. She chewed on that. "So an offer is anything a performer says or does that gives information about the scene," she said slowly, "like a place, a name, or a problem."

"Sure, whatever that's called," Marcus said, "but you ignored my offer and made me look weird instead. Try again." He picked up his invisible pole and cast it out.

Sofia leaned forward, gripping an imaginary edge, because if they were on a boat, the boat needed both of them. "Yes, and watch out, that thing you hooked is pulling us toward the rocks," she said. "Captain Sofia cannot lose her first catch."

Marcus widened his eyes. "It's not a fish. It's a predatory sea lion, and it's coming aboard."

"Then grab the cooler. We'll trade it our whole sandwich economy, every last crumb, before it eats the motor." She mimed hurling a sandwich, and he caught it and lobbed it back, and the sea lion grew more ridiculous with every throw until Mom shouted from the kitchen to please stop rocking the furniture.

They ran it twice more. Sofia deliberately tested her idea. Once she refused an offer, saying "there's no door there" when Marcus mimed opening one, and the scene collapsed into nothing, both of them standing around. Once she caught a place, a name, and a problem all at once, and the scene about two sisters trapped in a haunted bakery practically wrote itself. The pattern held every time: notice the offer, add to it, and the story rolled forward like a wheel.

On the night of the drama club meeting, her partner, a nervous kid named Dev, spread his arms wide and flapped them. Sofia recognized the shape of the wings instantly.

"Yes," she said, stepping up beside him, "and I'll be the copilot. Fasten your goggles, Mr. Dev. This zeppelin is about to transport us over the Alps."

activity: to describe how natural selection changed the beak shapes of finches on different islands
knowledge_domain: to describe how natural selection changed the beak shapes of finches on different islands
fact: Natural selection requires three things: individuals that vary, traits that are inherited, and some variations helping individuals survive and reproduce more than others.
story:
Alexandra knelt in the barn doorway with three tools laid out on a burlap sack: needle-nose pliers, a pair of chopsticks, and the fire tongs from the kitchen, which she had promised her mother she would return clean. Her little brother Milo crouched across from her, arms crossed.

"You said there'd be actual birds," Milo said.

"There are actual birds, on actual islands, far away. We're doing the next best thing." She poured a coffee can of mixed seeds between them: tiny flaxseeds, fat sunflower seeds, and a handful of dried beans. "These are different islands' food. The tools are different finch beaks."

"My scholarship book has finches," Milo said. He meant his library book, the one he carried around like a pet. "There's a picture. One beak is pointy and one is thick."

"Right. So here's my problem. I have to explain to my class why the beaks got different on each island, and I only get two minutes. I need to know if my idea actually works before I say it out loud." She picked up the pliers. "You're the chopstick beak. Ready? Go."

They grabbed seeds for thirty seconds, sorting what they "ate" into separate piles. The pliers cracked sunflower seeds easily. The chopsticks picked up flaxseeds one at a time. The beans mostly rolled away from both of them. Milo started laughing at the third bean that escaped him, and even Alexandra had to admit her pile looked ridiculous next to his heap of tiny seeds.

"Okay," she said, studying the piles. "On the flaxseed island, you survive and I starve. On the sunflower island, I survive and you starve. But wait." She frowned. "This just shows that beaks matter. That can't be the whole thing."

"Why not?"

"Because my teacher said we have to check three things before we can call it natural selection. I remember the list, but I have to make sure my finches pass all of it." She held up one finger. "First, the birds have to vary. My fake birds do, they have different beaks. Second, the beaks have to be inherited, meaning chicks get beaks like their parents." She tapped the chopsticks. "Third, some beaks have to help their owners survive and reproduce more than others. Survive and reproduce, both."

Milo squinted at the seed piles. "So on my island, the flaxseed birds have more chicks than the pliers birds."

"And their chicks have chopstick beaks," Alexandra said slowly. "Because it's inherited. So after lots of generations, that island is full of chopstick beaks, and nobody chose it. It just follows." She looked at the messy piles of seeds, then at Milo. "Say it back to me. All three parts."

"Variation, inherited, and the good beaks win."

"Close enough." She stood, brushed seed dust off her jeans, and grabbed the fire tongs. "One more island. Beans. Your turn to starve."

activity: to explain how the Treaty of Versailles helped lead to the Second World War
knowledge_domain: to explain how the Treaty of Versailles helped lead to the Second World War
fact: In March 1936, Hitler sent German troops into the Rhineland, breaking the Treaty of Versailles, and Britain and France did not use force to stop him.
story:
Grandpa's porch smelled like sawdust and lemon, and Jade spread her history notes across the table beside his coffee mug. Tomorrow she had to explain to her class how the Treaty of Versailles helped lead to the Second World War, and right now all she had was a page of dates that refused to stick together in her head.

"Still fighting with that treaty?" Grandpa asked, setting down a plate of sliced apples.

"It's like a list of rules some countries signed," Jade said. "And then I read one thing that confused me. In March 1936, Hitler sent German troops into the Rhineland, which broke the Treaty of Versailles. And Britain and France didn't use force to stop him." She frowned at her notes. "Why wouldn't they stop him right there? They had armies. He broke the rule in front of everybody."

Grandpa polished his watch, the old brass one that had belonged to his own father, and slid it across the table for her to hold, the way he always did, like a small ritual between them. "What do you think happens," he asked, "when a rule gets broken and nobody stops it?"

Jade turned the watch over in her hands, thinking. Then something clicked, and it wasn't from the book. Last month, Marcus Fenwick had eaten a granola bar in the library, which was against the rules, and Ms. Petrucci had been at the copier and never noticed. Jade had assumed somebody would catch him eventually. Two weeks later Marcus dragged an entire pizza into the library and set it on the atlas shelf, cheese and all, like he was testing whether the first time had counted. "The first time nobody stops you," she said slowly, "you find out the rule is softer than it looked. So you try something bigger."

She pulled her notebook closer and started sketching it out with arrows. Rule made after one war. Rule broken once, no consequences. Next break, bigger. She read the date again, March 1936, and wrote at the top of her page: nobody stops the first broken rule, so the next one gets bigger. It wasn't the whole answer, but it was a real thread, and she could follow it in front of the class tomorrow.

"Better," Grandpa said, reading over her shoulder. He tapped the watch in her palm. "That's hereditary, by the way. It goes to your mom, then someday to you. Keep it running and it won't fail you."

Jade wound the tiny knob until it resisted, then held it to her ear and listened to it tick, steady and small, like proof that some things keep going once you set them in motion.

activity: to stand up for a classmate being teased without making the situation worse
knowledge_domain: to stand up for a classmate being teased without making the situation worse
fact: A 2001 study that observed children on school playgrounds found that other children were present during 88 percent of bullying episodes.
story:
The bus smelled like wet boots and orange peel, and Rosalie was halfway through her grape soda when the laughing started. Derek had Wesley's notebook and was holding it above his head, reading Wesley's agriculture project out loud in a silly voice. "The cow's digestive system has four compartments," Derek announced. "Did you write this, Wes? Did the cow write it for you?"

Wesley reached for the notebook and missed. He didn't say anything, just turned red and stared at the floor. Last month, when Derek had called Wesley "Farmer Nobody" for a whole week, Rosalie had looked out the window too. She had told herself that getting involved would only give Derek a new target, and maybe that was true, or maybe it was just the excuse she handed herself every time.

She thought about something her cousin had told her after a playground research project he'd read about, that other kids were watching during 88 percent of bullying episodes. Ninety-three times out of a hundred, if you saw teasing, you were not the only one seeing it. She scanned the bus now and tested the idea. Kids in the back were smirking at their phones, pretending not to notice. Priya was frowning at her math homework, but her eyes kept flicking up. Even the eighth graders, who usually dismissed everything sixth graders did as beneath them, had gone quiet. Almost everybody was watching. That meant the problem wasn't that no one cared. It was that every single person was waiting for someone else to go first.

Rosalie stood up. Her legs felt like they belonged to someone else. She walked back, took the notebook out of Derek's loose grip, and set it on Wesley's lap. Then she sat down across the aisle, right between Wesley and Derek's audience, because a cousin's advice rattled in her head: be assertive, not loud. She kept her voice level.

"Four stomach compartments is actually interesting," she said. "Wesley's going to state with that project. Are you going to state with anything, Derek?"

Derek shrugged, but he had nothing, and everyone on the bus knew it. Somebody in the back snorted, and this time the laugh was aimed at Derek, not Wesley. Rosalie's heart hammered. That was the part she hadn't planned, the laugh turning like a weather vane.

Derek pulled his hood up and looked at his shoes. Priya lowered her homework and slid over to sit near Wesley, and a seventh grader asked him whether cows really chew twice. Wesley, still pink, started explaining.

Rosalie sipped her grape soda and watched the rain streak the windows. She wasn't sure she'd done it the right way, or even what the right way was. Maybe tomorrow Derek would be angrier. Maybe Wesley would rather she'd stayed out of it. But when the bus pulled up to the school, Wesley gathered his notebook, looked straight at her, and said, "Four compartments. Rumen, reticulum, omasum, abomasum."

"Save it for state," she said.

activity: to improvise a scene with a partner by accepting each offer with yes, and
knowledge_domain: to improvise a scene with a partner by accepting each offer with yes, and
fact: Viola Spolin's 1963 book 'Improvisation for the Theater' collected theater games and is often called the bible of improv teaching.
story:
Grandpa's porch smelled like sawdust and lemonade, and Levi had exactly one hour before the camp showcase started in the barn. His scene partner, Priya, kept throwing him lines and he kept shutting them down. When she said, "We're astronauts landing on Mars," he said, "No, we're at school." When she said, "Look, a dust storm," he said, "There isn't one." The scene died both times, flat as a dropped pancake.

The counselor, Marcus, flopped onto the porch swing and dug into his backpack. "Levi, you want to know why nothing's working? Watch." He held up a battered book with a cracked spine and a coffee ring on the cover. "Viola Spolin, 1963, 'Improvisation for the Theater.' It collected theater games, and people call it the bible of improv teaching. Everything we do at this camp revolves around it." He dropped it on Levi's knees. "There's a game in there for your exact problem. Find it, practice it, be in the barn by six."

Levi flipped pages while Priya read over his shoulder. He noticed a pattern in the games: every one made two players build on each other, never block. That had to be the hidden rule. He tested it out loud. "Okay, new plan. Whatever you say, I say yes, and then I add something." Priya squinted. "Like a treaty?" "Yeah, a treaty. We accept every offer, no matter how weird." She stuck out her hand and he shook it.

They ran the scene right there on the porch swing, cicadas buzzing in the hedge. "We're astronauts landing on Mars," Priya said. "Yes, and the dust storm is coming straight at us," Levi said. His heart hammered, but it worked, so he pushed further. "Yes, and the ship's computer is being obstinate and refuses to open the door." Priya laughed so hard she nearly fell off the swing, then fired back, "Yes, and the computer only opens for people who sing to it." They sang, badly, and Grandpa came out on the porch to see what the racket was.

At the showcase they did the Mars scene in front of forty folding chairs, and it went even better, because Levi caught himself about to say "no" when Priya claimed a Martian was knocking, and turned it into, "Yes, and it's holding our missing lunch." The crowd roared. Afterward, Marcus tapped the worn book under Levi's arm. "Keep it till the end of summer," he said. Levi opened it to the dog-eared page and read by barn light, one game at a time.

activity: to chop an onion safely with the claw grip and make a pasta sauce from scratch
knowledge_domain: to chop an onion safely with the claw grip and make a pasta sauce from scratch
fact: Garlic burns much faster than onion and tastes bitter when burnt, so many cooks add it only after the onions have softened.
story:
Ryder curled his fingers into a claw, knuckles forward, and set the blade against the onion the way the cooking video had shown him. If he cut the onion this way, his fingertips stayed out of the blade's path, and Mom, who got home at six thirty sharp, would walk into a kitchen that smelled like real sauce instead of the jar kind. His motive wasn't just dinner. She'd been working double shifts all week, and he wanted to hand her a plate of something she didn't have to make.

The onion fought him. It slid, it made his eyes stream, and his first slices came out as thick as door hinges. But by the second onion his claw grip felt steadier, and the pieces fell into even little cubes. He swept them into the pan, turned the heat up high to save time, and dumped in the minced garlic along with them, because garlic and onion went together, right?

The first batch of sauce tasted wrong. Ryder dipped a spoon in, blew on it, and frowned. Something underneath the sweet tomato was sharp and nasty, a burnt bitterness that clung to his tongue. He stared at the pan and thought it through like a puzzle. The onions had come out fine, golden and soft. The garlic, though, was dark at the edges, almost black. He hadn't seen it happen, but the evidence was sitting right there in the pan. Garlic must cook much faster than onion, and burnt garlic tasted bitter. He had thrown them in together on high heat, and the garlic had burned long before the onions were ready.

He scraped the batch into the compost bucket and checked the clock. Six ten. Twenty minutes, and Mom would be at the door. "Okay," he whispered to the pan. "Onions first. Garlic waits."

The second time, he lowered the heat and let the onions soften slowly, stirring while they turned translucent and sweet. Only then did he add the garlic, and he watched it closely, pulling the pan off the burner the moment it turned fragrant and pale gold. Canned tomatoes went in next, a pinch of salt, a pinch of sugar, and he let it all bubble while he boiled the pasta. His little sister wandered in, sniffing. "It smells like Nonna's kitchen," she said, and he let her stir once, carefully, with his hand over hers.

At six thirty two, keys rattled in the lock. Ryder slid the sauce onto the drained pasta, and the steam rose up rich and sweet with no bitterness anywhere. Mom stood in the doorway, coat still on, grocery bag dangling from her wrist. "You made this?" Ryder set the plate down in front of her and handed her a fork. "Taste it," he said.

activity: to draw a street using one-point perspective with lines meeting at a vanishing point
knowledge_domain: to draw a street using one-point perspective with lines meeting at a vanishing point
fact: Moving the horizon line up or down changes the view: a low horizon makes the street feel seen from a child's height, a high one from a window above.
story:
Stella crouched on the curb outside the art cabin with her sketchbook balanced on her knees, trying to make the camp's gravel lane look like it was racing away from her toward the lake. The art counselor had shown them one-point perspective that morning: two lines slanting inward, everything aimed at a single dot called the vanishing point. It had seemed like magic. Now her street looked like a squashed taco.

"You're smushing it," said Priya, plopping down beside her with a popsicle. "Mine looks way better, and I didn't even sit on the ground. I drew from the window in the loft above the canoe shed."

Stella leaned over. Priya's street was different in a way Stella couldn't name. The lane rose up tall and proud on the page, the cabins on either side stretching upward like towers, and the sky above it all was just a skinny ribbon. Stella's own drawing had almost no sky at all; hers was nearly all road, flopping up at her like a pancake flipped too soon.

They argued about whose street was right until Priya suggested they test it. Priya would retrieve her sketchbook from the loft, and Stella would draw the exact same lane from the exact same spot upstairs, without peeking at Priya's finished page. Then they would compare.

Up in the loft, Stella flattened her paper against the windowsill. The gravel lane looked smaller from up here, tidier, and when she drew her two slanting lines to their vanishing point, the horizon line landed high on her page, near the top, leaving that same skinny ribbon of sky. She ran downstairs holding it like a treasure. Side by side with Priya's, the two drawings looked like twins.

"But mine from the curb has the horizon way down low," Stella said slowly, staring at her first taco attempt. She grabbed the sketchbook and marched back to the curb, sat down, and drew the lane a third time, watching where her horizon landed. Low. Almost at the bottom of the page.

"That's it," she whispered. "A low horizon makes the street feel like a kid's view, like a mouse's view, standing right in the road. A high one feels like you're floating above, looking down from a window." She imagined a tiny artisan in a shop on that paper street, gluing miniature shingles onto miniature roofs, and she decided her parallel sidewalk edges would be so straight he could roll a marble all the way to the vanishing point without it wobbling.

She taped all three drawings to the cabin door: taco street from the curb, floating street from the loft, and her best one, a brand-new street drawn from a dragon's height, somewhere in between. Priya squinted at it. "That one looks like we're flying."

"We are," Stella said, and drew tiny wing shadows across the paper road.

activity: to explain how nicotine causes addiction in the brain's reward pathway
knowledge_domain: to explain how nicotine causes addiction in the brain's reward pathway
fact: When smoke is inhaled, nicotine reaches the brain within about 10 seconds.
story:
Naomi had signed up for canoeing, archery, and the camp newspaper, so nobody was more surprised than she was to be spending the last hour of the first day at the health cabin, listening to the camp nurse talk about the body. She had twisted her ankle on the dock steps, that was all, and while she iced it, a junior counselor named Priya sat across from her, waiting for her own checkup.

Priya was sixteen and looked competent and unbothered, the kind of person who could right a flipped canoe single-handedly, but her question came out quiet. "My uncle reaches for a cigarette the second anything stresses him. Like the doorbell rings and he's already lighting one. Why so fast? It's not like the smoke does something that quick."

Naomi couldn't stop thinking about it. That evening she found Priya at the lake and held up the health poster she'd borrowed from the nurse's bulletin board, the one with a big diagram of a brain and a path drawn through it like a hiking trail, labeled the reward pathway. "I looked it up in the nurse's reference shelf after you left," she said. "When smoke is inhaled, nicotine reaches the brain within about ten seconds."

Priya blinked. "Ten seconds? That's, like, nothing."

"Count it," Naomi said, and she pulled out the stopwatch she used for the newspaper's canoe races. Priya closed her eyes and started to describe her uncle getting a stressful phone call, and Naomi clicked the timer. At six seconds Priya said, "He's got the pack out." At ten she said, "He's inhaling." At fifteen, "He says he feels better." Naomi wrote it all in her notebook like it was race data, and she could hardly hold the pencil still. "So the good feeling arrives practically with the smoke. His brain learns that formula: something bad happens, smoke, feel better. The reward pathway fires, and the brain wants the shortcut again."

The next morning Naomi and Priya sat on the dock categorizing the uncle's triggers into a chart for the camp newspaper: stress, boredom, after meals, phone calls. When they were done, Priya laughed and said the uncle in question was, in fact, Camp Director Hughes, her mom's brother, who would be at the closing campfire on Friday. Naomi's mouth fell open. She had been writing about the man who ran the whole camp.

At the campfire, Priya handed him the notebook, chart and all, with the stopwatch clipped to the cover. He read it through once, then again, while the fire popped. "Ten seconds," he said finally. "And how long to quit?"

"That part I couldn't find a number for," Naomi admitted.

He closed the notebook and stood up. "Then I'll start counting something else instead." He walked the stopwatch straight to the nurse's cabin and knocked.

activity: to do a load of laundry from sorting colours to folding
knowledge_domain: to do a load of laundry from sorting colours to folding
fact: Dots on the iron symbol set the highest safe iron setting: one dot is low, about 110 degrees Celsius, two is medium, about 150, and three is high, about 200.
story:
Aubrey had two hours to kill every Tuesday while her mom taught driving lessons at Vega's Driving Academy, and the back room of the old converted gas station held a washer, a dryer, and an ironing board that Mrs. Vega used for the company uniforms. Mrs. Vega had finally agreed to let Aubrey run a whole load, which meant sorting the towels from the navy instructor shirts from Marcus's white shirt with red stripes. Marcus came every Tuesday too, waiting for his older sister, and he plopped his gym bag on the counter.

"That shirt has to be clean for Saturday," he said. "Race day. Coach says the whole team wears the matching ones." He pulled out a slippery gray shirt instead, some kind of costume nylon thing with a rocket on it. "And this got wrinkled in my closet, so it needs ironing, but careful, okay? It's my brother's."

Aubrey sorted carefully, remembered the red stripes could bleed into the whites if she got lazy about it, and started the washer. While it churned, she set up the iron. It had a dial marked linen, cotton, wool, and a low end with no name. She figured high heat was for serious wrinkles, so she clicked it to cotton and let it warm up. She flattened the gray shirt and pressed the rocket.

A hiss, a smell like warm plastic, and a shiny stiff patch spread across the fabric where the iron had sat. Marcus groaned. Aubrey lifted the iron and stared at the damage, then turned the shirt over to look at its tag. There was a little picture of an iron, and inside it, one single dot.

"Wait," she said, and dug through the drawer under the ironing board until she found a laminated care card Mrs. Vega kept there. She read it aloud. "Dots on the iron symbol set the highest safe iron setting: one dot is low, about 110 degrees Celsius, two is medium, about 150, and three is high, about 200." She checked the tag again, then the tags on the instructor shirts. "Your brother's shirt says one dot. That's the lowest setting there is. I had it on cotton, which is way up near the top of the dial."

Marcus was about to resign himself to a ruined shirt when Aubrey held the card next to the dial and found the little dot markings printed there, one dot, two dots, three, almost invisible in the worn plastic. She turned the dial down to one dot and waited, hand on the fabric of a test corner. It seemed strange that one small dot could carry so much information, and yet here was the evidence, shiny and stiff, on Marcus's brother's rocket. The card didn't say why. It just said what the dots meant, and that was the part she needed.

"You're going to wash my race shirt too, right?" Marcus asked, hovering. "It's resilient, it survives everything, but the stripes still count."

"I already sorted it separately," Aubrey said. The iron clicked softly at its low setting. She laid the gray shirt flat, kept the iron moving this time, and watched the wrinkles smooth out while the shiny patch stayed. Marcus leaned over her shoulder as the rocket straightened itself out, one careful pass at a time. "Tell your brother a tiny meteor hit it," Aubrey said, and pressed down on the next wrinkle.

activity: to compare a stock and a bond and explain which is riskier and why
knowledge_domain: to compare a stock and a bond and explain which is riskier and why
fact: A company can cut or skip the dividends it pays stockholders, but missing a promised interest payment on its bonds counts as a default.
story:
Victor poured the last of the pitcher into a paper cup and watched his sister Maya count her nickels on the upside-down milk crate she used as a chair. She had bought one share of GreenFrost Dairy with her birthday money because the company paid a small dividend every few months, and she had been planning to fold that money into her lemonade investment. This morning she had found a notice in her email. GreenFrost had cut its dividend to nothing.

"Zero," Maya said, sliding the phone across the crate so Victor could see. "They just stopped paying."

Victor looked at the screen, then at the jar of quarters under the register box, which held forty-one dollars of his own. He had been trying to decide for a week whether to buy a share of the same company or one of its bonds, and Maya's news made the choice feel suddenly urgent and confusing. Their older brother Theo owned a GreenFrost bond, and his interest payment had landed in his account that same morning, right on schedule. Same company, same week. One paid, one didn't.

Victor thought about the summer he and Theo had contracted to split the lemonade money evenly, and how the year before that he and Maya had agreed to split only the leftover profit after costs, which sometimes meant nothing at all. One promise had a shape you could hold; the other depended on how things went. He tested the idea out loud, spinning a nickel on the crate between them. "So Theo's bond is like our even split. It's a promised payment. Your stock is like the leftover-profit deal. If the company does badly, they can just cut it, and you can't do anything about it."

"That's what default means," Theo said, coming around the corner of the garage with two folding chairs. "If the bond missed a promised payment, the company would be in default. But the stock, they can cut that whenever they want." He set the chairs down next to a parliament of sparrows perched along the fence, who scattered at the clatter and resettled a moment later.

Victor spun the nickel again and let it wobble to a stop. "So the bond is the safer one," he said slowly. "Not because the company is better, but because the promise is stronger." He remembered the day he had chosen the leftover-profit deal with Maya because it sounded bigger, and how he had ended that summer with eight dollars while Theo walked away with twenty. He had told himself then that he would remember. He wasn't sure he had, until right now.

A spontaneous wave of customers arrived just then, three kids from the cross-country team, hot and loud, and Victor and Maya were suddenly pouring, making change, and shouting prices over each other. When the crowd thinned, Victor picked up the nickel and held it out to Maya. "Trade you," he said. "For the first nickel of whatever I end up with."

Maya closed her hand around it. "You're buying the bond, aren't you."

Victor tucked the jar of quarters under his arm and headed inside to get his shoes. "I'm buying the bond."

activity: to compare the climate of a desert and a rainforest using rainfall and temperature graphs
knowledge_domain: to compare the climate of a desert and a rainforest using rainfall and temperature graphs
fact: Parts of Chile's Atacama Desert are so dry that some weather stations there have never recorded rain.
story:
The clock above the whiteboard gave them twenty minutes, and Aubrey's graph still had a hole in it. Her assignment was to build a climate graph for a desert and one for a rainforest, comparing rainfall bars and temperature lines, and then present both to the class. The rainforest side was finished, green bars stacked tall month after month. The desert side, the Atacama in Chile, was almost empty.

"Mine's broken," said Marcus, who shared her table. He held up his own graph. "Half my rainfall bars won't draw. I keep getting nothing for January, March, July, everything."

Aubrey leaned over. "Mine too. Watch." She entered the rainfall number for June and pressed the key. The space where the bar should have been stayed blank. She tried September, then December, then every single month, one after another, and not one bar appeared. "It's not broken. There's nothing to draw."

"That can't be right," Marcus said. "Every place gets rain sometimes. Even a desert. Right?"

Aubrey stared at the flat white space. A rule had to be hiding underneath the data, some pattern she couldn't see directly, and the only way to find it was to test it. She grabbed a fresh data sheet and ran her pencil down the station's numbers. Every rainfall box was blank. Not zero written in, not a smudge, just blank, all year, every year the sheet covered.

"Marcus," she said slowly, "what if the bars are missing because the rain never happened? What if some weather stations in the Atacama have never recorded rain at all?"

Marcus blinked. "Never? Like, never ever?"

"That's what the sheet says. Never." She checked another sheet from a different station, and that one had a few thin bars, which meant the first station wasn't just a printing error. Some stations showed rain and some showed none, and hers was one of the ones with none. Her graph wasn't broken. It was telling the truth.

"Then how do you present a graph with nothing on it?" Marcus asked. He slid his chair closer. "Mr. Reyes will think we skipped the work."

"You put the bars that belong there, and then you show why the rest are gone." Aubrey picked up her pencil and wrote along the empty bottom of her graph, right where the missing months were: no rainfall recorded at this station, ever. Then she labeled her two graphs side by side. The rainforest's temperature line stayed warm and steady while its rainfall bars towered. The Atacama's line rose and fell with the seasons, but the rainfall row lay flat and bare, emptier than anything else on the wall.

When Mr. Reyes called time, Aubrey went first. She held up both graphs, and before she could speak, a boy in the second row named Dev, who never volunteered anything, raised his hand halfway.

"Is yours messed up?" he asked. "The one on the right has, like, no bars."

"That's the desert," Aubrey said. "Parts of the Atacama are so dry that some weather stations there have never recorded rain."

The room went quiet. Dev sat forward, and Marcus whispered, "Tell them about the decomposers."

Aubrey nodded and pointed at the rainforest graph. "All that rain means dead leaves rot fast, so decomposers, the bugs and fungi that break things down, are everywhere there. In the Atacama, without rain, even that barely happens." She turned back to the flat white row. "I thought my graph was broken at first. Then I tested every month. It wasn't broken. That empty space is the most important part."

Mr. Reyes wrote something on his clipboard, and Dev raised his hand again. "Can I see the sheets?"

activity: to look at onion skin cells under a microscope and label the cell wall, membrane and nucleus
knowledge_domain: to look at onion skin cells under a microscope and label the cell wall, membrane and nucleus
fact: In a healthy onion cell, the cell membrane is pressed tightly against the inside of the cell wall, which makes the membrane very hard to see as a separate line.
story:
Naomi had been warned that the barn after dark belonged to the barn owl, but she went in anyway, carrying her grandfather's microscope case and an onion from the kitchen basket. The science packet was due Monday, and the worksheet demanded three labels: cell wall, cell membrane, nucleus. She set the microscope on the workbench near the window where the porch light spilled in, and the owl above her shifted its weight but did not cease its silent watching. Nocturnal things hunt at night, her grandmother always said, so Naomi kept her movements small.

She had watched her cousin peel a paper-thin layer of onion skin once, so she tried it the same way, snapping the onion in half and teasing off a strip so thin it was almost invisible. She laid it on a slide, added a drop of water, and pressed the cover glass down. Through the lens at low power, the cells looked like bricks in a wall, neat rectangles lined up row after row. The outer edge of each brick was bold and dark. She wrote cell wall on her drawing and felt pleased with herself.

The nucleus took longer. She switched to high power and hunted through the field of pale gray until she found one cell with a dense round spot near the middle, like a pebble under ice. She labeled it. Then she sat back and read the last line of the worksheet again. Label the cell membrane. She looked. She looked for a long time. There was the wall, thick and certain, and inside it nothing but cytoplasm and that lone round nucleus. No second line. Nothing to point to.

The suspense got under her skin. Maybe onion cells simply did not have membranes. Maybe the packet had a mistake in it, and everyone in her class would write impossible on their sheets. She imagined turning it in blank and Mrs. Okafor's pen hovering. But before she decided anything, an idea came to her, small and testable. If the membrane were a real thing in there, maybe it was hidden because it was pressed tight against the wall, so close they looked like one line. If that were true, then a cell whose wall had been damaged or wrinkled might show the membrane pulled away, a second thin line where the two had separated.

She searched the slide near the torn edge of her onion strip, where the peel had folded and crumpled. There, in a bent cell, she saw it: a delicate inner line had peeled back from the dark outer one, like a glove slipping away from a coat sleeve. She grabbed a fresh strip, tore it deliberately along one side, and found it again in a second cell. In a healthy cell, the membrane hugged the wall so tightly that she could never have seen it as a separate line. She drew both cells side by side, labeled all three parts, and underlined the membrane twice.

Above her, the owl dropped from the rafter, swept once through the doorway, and vanished into the dark field. Naomi held her slide up to the porch light and smiled at it. "Found you," she said.

activity: to compare simple and compound interest on a savings account over five years
knowledge_domain: to compare simple and compound interest on a savings account over five years
fact: At the same yearly rate, interest compounded monthly grows a little faster than interest compounded yearly, because each month's interest starts earning sooner.
story:
Naomi had forty-two dollars and a plan to double it, so when two bank flyers slid out of the Sunday paper, she spread them across the kitchen table like treasure maps. Both banks promised 3 percent interest on savings accounts. "They're the same," her brother Theo said, grabbing the last toaster waffle. "Just pick the one with the free water bottle."

"You pick the water bottle," Naomi said. "I want the one that pays more." The flyers were not quite the same, though both said 3 percent. Riverside Bank said interest compounded yearly. First Corner said interest compounded monthly. She said the word "compounded" out loud twice, testing it. Theo shrugged and went to find the remote.

She provoked an argument on purpose at dinner, just to get information. "Dad, if two banks both pay 3 percent, they'd give you the same money, right?" Dad carved the roast chicken and smiled like she'd set a trap for herself. "What do you think?" Naomi hated that answer. It meant work.

After dinner she called her cousin Marisol, who was fifteen and had an actual savings account with actual statements. Marisol texted back a screenshot of her bank statement and then a message: "mine compounds monthly. after 5 yrs my statement shows a tiny bit more than my friend's at the same rate. same rate, both banks, hers yearly. i checked twice." Naomi read it four times. The numbers were right there, small but real: monthly came out ahead.

She wanted to see it happen herself, not just be told. So she took her mom's calculator, an old one with a sticky zero button, and pretended her forty-two dollars stayed in each bank for five years. She stepped through the monthly version first, adding a small bit of interest twelve times a year, then letting that new total earn the next bit. Then she did the yearly version, adding interest once each year. Her fingers got tired and Theo wandered through and asked if the calculator was a toy. "It's science," she said, and shielded it with her arm. At the end, the monthly pile stood a little taller than the yearly one. Not much. A few cents. But it won.

She checked her work twice, and both times the result was consistent, so she made her inference: at the same rate, monthly compounding beat yearly. She couldn't see the money growing, exactly, but she could see the pattern in the numbers, and the pattern pointed one direction. On Monday after school she marched to First Corner with her forty-two dollars in a zippered pouch. The teller, a young woman named Priya, slid a form across the counter. "Who helped you pick us?" she asked. "My cousin's statement," Naomi said, unzipping the pouch, "and a calculator with a sticky zero."

activity: to improvise a scene with a partner by accepting each offer with yes, and
knowledge_domain: to improvise a scene with a partner by accepting each offer with yes, and
fact: Keith Johnstone's 1979 book 'Impro' taught that characters in a scene play higher or lower status, and shifting status creates drama.
story:
Carter's audition for the fall play was in three days, and the notice said one word he did not like: improvise. He had memorized a monologue for nothing. Now he would have to make up a scene with a partner, on the spot, in front of everyone.

In the kitchen, his older sister Priya was eating cereal and reading a battered paperback called "Impro," written by Keith Johnstone in 1979. She had gotten it from the library because she wanted to be funny. "There's stuff in here about scenes," she said, pushing it across the table. "You can read it if you want."

Carter read until his cereal went soggy. One idea jumped out at him. In a scene, characters play higher or lower status, and shifting status creates drama. The servant who suddenly gives orders to the king makes everyone laugh. He wondered if that could really work. It felt like a rule for something invisible, like the reason a joke works or doesn't. You couldn't see status itself, only what people did with it. He decided to test it.

"Be my partner," he said to Priya. "You're the king. I'm the servant."

Priya put down her spoon and sat up very straight. "Servant! Bring me my crown. Polish it with your sleeve."

"Yes, Your Majesty." Carter bowed low, shuffled backward, kept his eyes on the floor. He fetched an invisible crown and held it out with trembling hands. It was strangely fun to be small.

Then, on a hunch, he straightened up. "Your crown is smudged, and frankly you've been wearing it crooked for weeks. Also, you're late for the council meeting, and I've rescheduled it without asking you."

Priya's mouth twitched. "You rescheduled my council meeting?"

"I did. And you'll be eating boiled vegetables tonight. Doctor's orders." He pointed at her plate. "That's your second bowl of cereal."

Priya cracked up so hard she had to put the spoon down. "Okay, okay. Why is that so much funnier when you boss me around?" Carter didn't have a full answer, but he had noticed the pattern: the scene only came alive when the statuses started to shift. A king and servant who stayed fixed felt flat, like a drawing of a scene instead of a scene.

They tried again, trading who got to be the protagonist. Carter played a pilot whose passenger, Priya, kept taking over the controls, and Priya played a student whose janitor began assigning her homework. Every time, the same thing happened: the moment the low character rose, or the high character shrank, the kitchen filled with laughter.

At the audition, Carter drew a girl named Maya as his partner. The director said, "Your scene: two strangers stuck in an elevator." Maya started as the confident one, pressing buttons and announcing they would be fine. Carter began low, nervous, apologizing for breathing too loudly. Then he remembered the cereal-soggy morning and let his voice steady. "Actually, sit down. We're going to wait, and you're going to share your granola bar, because I skipped breakfast and you've been hiding it in your pocket since the doors closed." Maya's eyes went wide, and then she grinned, sat down on the floor of the imaginary elevator, and broke the granola bar in half.

activity: to compare a first-past-the-post election with proportional representation using a sample vote count
knowledge_domain: to compare a first-past-the-post election with proportional representation using a sample vote count
fact: French political scientist Maurice Duverger observed that first-past-the-post elections tend to produce two large parties, an idea now called Duverger's law.
story:
Nevaeh spread the sticky notes across Grandpa's kitchen table in three columns: Orange Party, Blue Party, Green Party. Each note was a vote from her class's mock election on where to go for the field trip, and she had copied the results onto the notes so she could move them around.

"There's the problem," she said, tapping the Orange column, which held twelve notes. Blue held eleven and Green held seven. "Orange wins the whole thing, even though nineteen kids voted against the aquarium and only twelve voted for it. That's how our class vote worked, and I want to know if there's a better way to count."

Grandpa set down his coffee mug and pulled a chair around beside her. "So move the notes. Show me another way."

Nevaeh slid the thirty notes into three equal rows of ten, then squinted at them. "What if it were proportional? If there were ten seats on the field trip committee, Orange would get four, Blue four, Green two. Nobody's shut out." She stacked them back into columns and stared. "But here's what I keep wondering. Why does Green never win anything, in our class or in real elections? Are Green voters just rare, or is something else going on?"

She grabbed a fresh sticky note and wrote a guess on it: Maybe smaller parties lose because the counting method squeezes them out, not because people don't vote for them. Then she tested it. She pretended the class voted again, but this time everyone who wanted Green had to pick between Orange and Blue, because in first-past-the-post, the winner just needs more votes than anyone else. Green's seven notes vanished into the other two piles, and the big columns grew.

"Grandpa, look. If we do it this way, over and over, the small party stops existing. The two big ones just eat everybody." She assumed the same thing happened in real countries, so she asked him to look it up, and he fetched his laptop and typed while she rearranged the notes into a neat pyramid, two giants at the bottom.

"There's a name for what you just found," Grandpa said, turning the screen toward her. "A French political scientist, Maurice Duverger, observed that first-past-the-post elections tend to produce two large parties."

"It's called Duverger's law," Nevaeh read aloud, saying the name slowly, twice, until it sat right in her mouth. She wrote it at the top of her pyramid. "So it's not that people don't want a third choice. It's the counting."

She sat back, tapping her pencil against the table. "So in a proportional system, would our Green Party still be around? Would it be durable, like, still winning seats years from now?" She imagined a Green dynasty, Green mayors and Green class presidents, a whole line of them, and she laughed at the picture in her head.

Then she folded the pyramid flat, tucked the sticky notes into her backpack next to her math binder, and headed for the door. "Monday, I'm making everybody vote twice."

activity: to stand up for a classmate being teased without making the situation worse
knowledge_domain: to stand up for a classmate being teased without making the situation worse
fact: Saving screenshots of hurtful online messages gives a trusted adult a record to act on, since messages can be deleted later.
story:
Evelyn sat on her grandmother's porch steps with her tablet balanced on her knees, squinting at the group chat for Mr. Ruiz's class project team. "Grandma," she called through the screen door, "if someone writes something mean and then deletes it, did it ever really happen?"

Grandma came out drying her hands on a dish towel. "Did what happen?"

Evelyn turned the tablet around. Three hours ago, a boy named Dev had posted a joke in the chat, and Dana, who never talked much at school, had replied with an answer that was a little off. Someone named Travis had written "wow, Dana can't even read" with a row of crying-laughing faces. Then the message had vanished. Evelyn had seen it. Dana, apparently, had not.

"That's like a footprint in wet cement that smooths itself out," Grandma said, tapping her chin. "How would you prove someone walked there?"

Evelyn chewed the edge of her thumbnail. She wondered whether screenshots worked the way she imagined, like pressing a pause button on the screen. She swiped back to the chat, found Travis's next message still sitting there, and pressed the buttons that captured the image. The tablet made a sound like a tiny camera shutter. She tried it on the whole thread, then scrolled up, hunting for anything else Travis had missed deleting.

"Smart girl," Grandma said. "Now, what's your plan? Don't delegate the hard part to me, this is your project team."
