The next morning Evelyn found Dana by the lockers, fiddling with a synthetic snake that was supposed to be for their science presentation. "Can it really shed its skin?" Evelyn asked, watching the rubbery tail coil around Dana's finger.

"Mine can't," Dana said. "It's plastic. But real ones do it all at once, in one piece."

"Like proof," Evelyn said, and explained about the deleted message and the screenshots she'd saved. Dana's eyes went wide. "I can show Mr. Ruiz?"

"You can show him together," Evelyn said. "Not to get Travis in trouble for its own sake. Just so he knows it happened." She'd thought about it all night, a small negotiation with herself: tattling made things worse, but staying silent made Dana alone. Showing a teacher the record was the road in between.

Mr. Ruiz looked at the screenshots for a long moment. Then he looked up at both of them.

"Thank you," he said. "This helps."

When Evelyn got home, Grandma was on the porch with two glasses of lemonade. "Well?"

Evelyn held up her tablet, the screenshots still glowing on the screen. "Proof," she said, "in one piece."

activity: to explain how the tilt of Earth's axis causes the seasons
knowledge_domain: to explain how the tilt of Earth's axis causes the seasons
fact: Earth's axis is tilted about 23.4 degrees from straight up relative to the plane of its orbit around the Sun.
story:
Matteo climbed down the quarry steps with a basketball under one arm and a flashlight in his back pocket, careful to keep his footing stable on the loose gravel. He was supposed to give his talk to the astronomy guild tonight, five whole minutes on why we have seasons, and he still didn't believe his own notes. His notes said seasons happened because Earth is closer to the Sun in summer. It sounded right. Closer meant hotter, the way standing closer to a campfire meant warmer hands.

At the bottom of the quarry, his friend Dana was waiting by the flooded pit, the part everyone called the blue pool because the water refracted the light until it glowed like a piece of sky. "Did you fix your talk?" she asked. Matteo shook his head. "I keep thinking about the globe at the planetarium," he said. "It was leaning. Like somebody bumped it and nobody straightened it out."

Dana frowned. "Maybe nobody bumped it." She pulled out her phone and found the little plaque from the planetarium display, the one they'd both walked past on the field trip. Matteo read it twice, then a third time. Earth's axis was tilted about 23.4 degrees from straight up relative to the plane of its orbit around the Sun. That was on purpose. That was how Earth actually was, all the time, forever. "So the globe isn't broken," he said slowly. "It's accurate."

He set the basketball on a flat rock and jammed a stick through a hole in the rubber so it stood out the top like an axis. Then he tilted the stick, holding it at the angle he remembered, and aimed the flashlight straight at the ball from the side, the way sunlight would come at Earth as it traveled around. He spun the ball slowly. When the top half leaned toward the light, the beam spread out in a wide, generous oval across the upper half, and the lower half got only a slanted, stretched sliver. When he turned the ball halfway around, still tilted the same way, it flipped. The south got the wide oval. "There it is," Matteo said. "It's not distance. It's the lean. Whichever half is tipped toward the light gets summer, and the same amount of light concentrates on a smaller patch, so it heats up more."

"So your whole first draft was wrong," Dana said. "Completely wrong," Matteo said, and he was grinning now, scribbling on the back of his notes. That night at the guild meeting, he stood the basketball on the table, tilted the stick, and clicked on the flashlight. "Watch the oval," he said. "This is summer. Now watch."

activity: to paint a portrait in watercolour by layering washes from light to dark
knowledge_domain: to paint a portrait in watercolour by layering washes from light to dark
fact: In traditional transparent watercolour, the brightest highlights, like the shine in an eye, are usually made by leaving the white paper unpainted rather than adding white paint.
story:
Aria set her folding table under the backyard maple and taped a sheet of watercolour paper to a board. Her subject sat across from her on an overturned bucket: her little brother Theo, who wanted more than anything to be painted looking like a knight.

"Layer by layer," she reminded herself, mixing a pale wash the colour of weak tea. Her art camp instructor had said to work from light to dark, saving the darkest darks for last, but she'd been too busy thinking about armor to write anything else down. She brushed the first wash over Theo's face and watched it dry in the sun.

The pale layer became a medium one, cheeks and freckles, then shadow under the chin. Theo held still for almost nine minutes, which for him was a record. "Am I heroic yet?" he asked. "Not yet," Aria said. "Right now you look like a person who smelled something bad." He grinned, and she painted the grin.

She was on the eyes, laying in the grey-blue of the iris, when she saw it. The paint covered everything, the whole eye, all of it. The paper had been white at the start, and now there was no white left in that eye at all. She tried adding white paint from her little tube, but it sat on top like toothpaste, chalky and dull, nothing like a gleam. She frowned at the portrait, then at Theo's actual eye, where a small bright spark sat near the pupil.

She thought back to the demo at camp, the instructor painting a robin, leaving bits of paper bare. The shine hadn't been painted on. The shine had been the paper itself, saved, kept white from the very beginning. That was the trick, and she had painted over her only chance at it. She felt like kicking the bucket Theo was sitting on, but instead she allocated the rest of her afternoon to a second painting, because the first one could not be undone. "New plan," she announced. "Sit back down. And don't sneeze."

Before she touched brush to paper, she studied where the light landed. One small dot in each eye, a sliver along the nose, a bright edge on the helmet she would paint around Theo's head. She mapped them with a tiny circle of plain pencil, then worked her washes around them like a river going around stones. Theo's friend Marcus came through the gate, saw the ruined first portrait, and squinted at it. "That's the irony of it," Marcus said. "The brightest part's made out of nothing." Aria laughed. "Paper. The brightest parts are just unpainted paper." Marcus wanted a portrait too, so he dragged over the recycling bin to sit on, though he insisted on being painted as aggressive-looking, like a dragon.

By suppertime the second Theo was dry, freckles and all, with two live eyes gleaming up out of the white paper, and a knight's helmet that shone along one edge. Theo held it at arm's length and then closer, then at arm's length again. "This one," he said, "looks like he could fight a whole army." Aria signed her name small in the corner and handed Marcus her palette. "You're next," she said. "Wash, wait, wash. And whatever you do, save your whites."

activity: to play a piece with dynamics and tempo changes in a band or on the piano
knowledge_domain: to play a piece with dynamics and tempo changes in a band or on the piano
fact: The marking 'a tempo' tells players to return to the original speed after the music has slowed down or sped up.
story:
The rehearsal room behind the concert hall smelled like dust and old curtains, and Rose's hands were sweating on the piano keys. She had practiced the recital piece for six weeks, but every time she reached the spot marked "rit." she fell apart afterward. She slowed down beautifully, exactly the way her teacher wanted, and then she kept dragging, slower and slower, until the ending collapsed like a wet paper bag.

She stopped and stared at the sheet music. The measure after the slow part had two small words printed above it: "a tempo." She had seen them a hundred times and never really looked. Her eyes moved back to "rit." and forward again. Slow down, then the two words, then the music looked the same as before. She flipped to the second page, where the same thing happened, and then to her duet partner Marcus's trumpet part, and there they were again in the same spots.

"Marcus," she said, "when you see those words, 'a tempo,' what do you do?"

"My brother says it means go back to your original speed," Marcus said, wiping his trumpet with a rag. "You know, after you've slowed down or sped up."

Rose set her metronome to the tempo from the beginning and played just that section, counting out loud. When she hit "rit." she eased off, let the notes stretch, and then at "a tempo" she snapped back to the click of the metronome. It worked. The slow part suddenly sounded like a valley between two hills instead of a hole she kept falling into.

She thought of the recital last spring, when she had played a different piece for her grandmother and the whole middle section had dragged. Grandma had called it "thoughtful," which Rose now understood was a kind lie. Back then she'd blamed her nerves, but sitting here she realized the truth was simpler and stranger: the answer had been printed on the page the entire time, invisible to her because she hadn't known what question to ask. It was like doing an analysis of a magic trick and finding out the trick was never hidden, only unread.

"Play it with me," she said to Marcus. "From the top."

They played together, and when the slow passage came, Rose leaned into it, then lifted out clean and bright on the other side. Marcus grinned over his trumpet. Then came the twist: at the very end of the piece Rose found "rit." printed above the final chord, with no "a tempo" after it at all.

"Look," she said, tapping the page. "This one's real. We're supposed to stay slow."

Marcus raised his trumpet. "Then let's take our time," he said.

activity: to do a load of laundry from sorting colours to folding
knowledge_domain: to do a load of laundry from sorting colours to folding
fact: Laundry is sorted by colour because new dark or bright clothes can release dye into the wash water, and that dye can tint white and pale clothes.
story:
Lucy fed quarters into the washer while her little brother Theo watched from the folding counter, swinging his legs. Mom was working late, the basket was full, and Lucy needed her white school shirt clean for the assembly tomorrow morning. She had promised Mom she could handle a whole load by herself, and she planned to prove it.

"First we sort," Lucy said, dumping the basket onto the counter. She made three piles: darks, brights, and whites. Theo picked up a brand new red sock, still stiff from the package, and held it up like a flag. "Can this go with the whites? There's only one sock." Lucy hesitated. It was just one sock, tiny against a whole pile. But the sock was new, and something about the way its color hadn't faded yet made her suspicious. She dropped it in with the darks instead, and Theo groaned like she had ruined his whole day.

While the first load spun, Theo wanted a snack from the vending machine, but they only had enough quarters for the dryer. "We have to compromise," Lucy said. "You can have the granola bar in my backpack now, and I'll owe you the vending machine next time." Theo considered this, then bit into the bar. "This is basically all carbohydrate," he said, reading the wrapper with his mouth full. "Good laundry fuel." Lucy laughed and promised herself she'd never tell his friends he said that.

The second load was the whites, and Lucy watched the water tumble through the little window, drumming her fingers. She was thinking about her white shirt from two months ago, the one that had come out pale pink after a wash. At the time she had blamed the detergent, but now she remembered something else in that load: a new red t-shirt. She couldn't see any dye in the water today, no pink clouds, nothing. But the shirt had turned pink anyway, back then, and the red sock today was new too. She stared at the sock sitting in the dark pile and felt like a detective who had finally matched a clue.

"That sock," she said slowly, "was in with my shirt before, I bet. New red stuff makes the water pink, and the pink gets into the whites." Theo shrugged. "Invisible pink. Spooky." But Lucy kept turning the idea over, deciding that from now on she'd sort new darks and brights away from whites every single wash, because the effect could be cumulative, each new red thing a little risk.

The dryer buzzed just as headlights swept the parking lot. Mom waved through the window. Lucy pulled the shirt out warm, still perfectly white, and folded it in sharp squares while Theo folded towels into lumpy balls. She held the shirt up to show Mom coming through the door. "Not a speck of pink," Lucy said. Theo patted the red sock in his pocket. "Invisible pink," he whispered, "stopped by me and Lucy."

activity: to explain how a river carves a canyon over millions of years through erosion and deposition
knowledge_domain: to explain how a river carves a canyon over millions of years through erosion and deposition
fact: In a canyon wall, harder rock layers tend to form steep cliffs and softer layers wear back into gentler slopes, which gives the Grand Canyon its stepped walls.
story:
Henry had one week to build a model that showed how a river could carve a canyon over millions of years, and he intended to win the sixth-grade science showcase with it. The controversy in Mr. Okoye's class had started on Monday, when Dante declared that no river was patient enough to cut through rock. "Water just splashes," Dante said. "It can't dig."

"It doesn't dig," Henry said. "It erodes. It carries the rock away, bit by bit, and drops it somewhere downstream. That's deposition." Dante looked unconvinced, so Henry decided to prove it.

He built a long plastic tray on a slight tilt and filled it with alternating layers. He packed half of them with damp clay he had baked until it was stiff, and half with loose, crumbly sand. Then he propped a jug above the high end and let a thin trickle of water run down the middle, and he waited.

For two days nothing much happened. The trickle wiggled sideways, nudged grains of sand along, and left a tiny fan of pale sediment at the low end of the tray, which Henry recognized as deposition in action. On the third morning he leaned close and noticed something he had not expected. The sand layers had worn back into gentle slopes, like ramps. The baked clay layers still stood out, stubborn and steep, forming little ledges. When he squinted, the whole cut looked like a staircase.

"Whoa," he whispered. He called his sister in. "Look at the walls. The hard layers make cliffs and the soft layers make slopes. That's why the walls look stepped." He grabbed the library book on the Grand Canyon and flipped through it until he found a photograph. The real canyon walls were stepped exactly like his model, cliffs and slopes stacked all the way down.

At the showcase, Dante stood by the tray with his arms crossed, defiant as ever. "Your river is a dribble," he said. "The Grand Canyon is enormous."

Henry pointed at the photograph, then at the tray, then at the chalky fan of sediment at the bottom. "Millions of years of dribble," he said. "And look at the walls in the picture. Hard rock holds up as cliffs. Soft rock wears back into gentler slopes. Stepped walls, just like mine." He touched the top ledge of clay, and a single grain of sand rolled down the little slope below it and vanished into the water.

Dante leaned in until his nose almost touched the tray, watching the trickle nudge another grain loose.

"How long did that take?" he asked.

"Three days," Henry said. "Imagine three days times a few million."

Dante picked up the jug and refilled it without being asked.

activity: to spot foreshadowing and symbolism in a short story and explain what they suggest
knowledge_domain: to spot foreshadowing and symbolism in a short story and explain what they suggest
fact: In James Hurst's 1960 story The Scarlet Ibis, a storm-blown red bird dies in the family garden, foreshadowing the fate of the fragile boy Doodle.
story:
Ava slid The Scarlet Ibis across the library table like it might bite her. "Mrs. Ruiz wants us to find one example of foreshadowing and one of symbolism by Friday," she told Marcus, who was balancing a pencil on his nose. "In a story this short. That's like hiding an elephant in a lunchbox."

Marcus dropped the pencil. "Then look for something weird. Teachers love weird." He flipped her book open to a page and stabbed a finger at it. "See? Bizarre. A red bird blows in with a storm and just keels over in their garden. What kind of bird does that?"

Ava read the page twice. The bird was exhausted, ragged, far from home, and it died right there among the flowers while the family watched. Something tickled at the back of her brain. She flipped forward a few pages to where Doodle, the small, fragile brother, was running through the rain, and then she flipped back again, comparing. The bird was red. Doodle, when he was born, had a red, shriveled body, and the story had said so almost in the same words. "Wait," she said slowly. "The bird is red and far from home and weak. Doodle is red and weak and everybody said he wouldn't survive. The two of them correspond. Like the story is sending me a postcard that says something bad is coming."

"So the bird is, what, a warning label?" Marcus picked the pencil back up. "Like when you get a concussion in gym and the coach says watch for signs later?"

"Kind of, except the sign comes first." Ava grabbed a sticky note and wrote storm, red bird, garden, dies, then drew an arrow. She tested her idea against the ending, where Doodle runs through a storm and falls, and the older brother finds him under a bush, red all over, in the garden. The bird's death and Doodle's death matched, piece for piece. Her skin prickled. "It's foreshadowing," she said. "The bird dying in the storm foreshadows what happens to Doodle later. And the ibis is a symbol too, because it stands for him. Fragile. Out of place. Trying so hard."

"That's actually kind of brilliant," Marcus admitted. "Also kind of depressing."

"It's brilliant and depressing." Ava stood up so fast her chair squeaked across the tile, and the librarian glared at them over her glasses. Ava whispered, "I'm going to write it on the board at home. Storm at the start, storm at the end. Bird, then Doodle." She stuffed the book in her bag, still open to the sticky note. "Marcus, if I get an A on this, I'm naming my next pet after you."

"Name it Doodle," he called after her, much too loud, and then he ducked behind the shelf as the librarian started toward their table.

activity: to build a web page with HTML and style it with CSS so the heading is centred
knowledge_domain: to build a web page with HTML and style it with CSS so the heading is centred
fact: When two CSS rules of equal specificity set the same property, the one written later wins; this ordering is part of the cascade in Cascading Style Sheets.
story:
Paisley slid her laptop toward the corner of the pit table, next to a bin of screws and a spare propeller for the team's flying demo bot. The Maplewood Middle robotics competition ran all day, and every team had to post a live results page so judges could check scores between rounds. Paisley had volunteered to build it, even though she had never written HTML before Saturday. She had learned fast, mostly by copying, pasting, and hoping.

The page worked, mostly. Her heading, MAPLEWOOD MECHATRONICS, sat stubbornly against the left edge of the screen, and she could not make it move. She had written text-align: center right at the top of her style sheet, under the rule for h1. She had checked the spelling four times. It was centered in her mind, so why not on the screen?

Her teammate Nadia leaned over, holding the team schedule against the table edge to fan herself. The gym was hot and smelled like solder and popcorn. "Round three is in ten minutes," Nadia said. "Judges look at the page right after we run. Want me to cover for you so you can fix it?"

"I've got ten minutes," Paisley said. "Go get Dev ready."

She scrolled through her CSS again, line by line. Halfway down, buried in a section she had copied from a tutorial site weeks ago, she spotted a second rule for h1. It said text-align: left. Her rule and this one both targeted h1, and this one sat lower in the file. She squinted at it, an idea forming. What if the page read the rules top to bottom, and the last thing it heard stuck?

She tested it the simplest way she could. She deleted nothing. Instead she copied her center rule, pasted it at the very bottom of the style sheet, and refreshed the browser. The heading glided to the middle of the page and stayed there, like it had finally been asked properly. Paisley sat back so fast she nearly knocked the propeller off the table.

"So the lower one wins," she said out loud when Nadia came back with two juice boxes and set one by Paisley's elbow without being asked.

"If they're both for the same thing, yeah," Nadia said. "It's called the cascade."

"The cascade," Paisley repeated, typing a comment into her file so she would remember. She decided to eliminate the duplicated rules entirely, keeping one clean center rule at the bottom, because a page with two rules fighting over the same heading felt like a robot with two drivers.

Round three started with a buzzer. Dev sent the bot across the field, and it stacked its blocks perfectly, which meant their dinosaur-themed decor, the paper T-Rex Dev insisted was "not extinct, just retired," would stay taped to the pit wall another round. When the judges came by with clipboards, the results page glowed on the laptop with the team name centered at the top like a real website. One judge tapped the screen and said, "Nice page. Who built it?"

Paisley raised her hand, a smear of solder flux still on her knuckles. "Still under construction," she said, and turned the laptop so the whole team could see their name shining in the middle.

activity: to build a spreadsheet with a formula that adds a column and makes a bar chart
knowledge_domain: to build a spreadsheet with a formula that adds a column and makes a bar chart
fact: A bar chart whose value axis starts above zero makes small differences look much bigger than they really are.
story:
Parker had been staying at Grandpa's house for a week, and so far the best part was the nightly card tournament. Grandpa, Aunt Rosa, and Parker kept score on a crumpled napkin, and Aunt Rosa was winning by just a few points. On Saturday morning, Grandpa handed Parker a laptop and a challenge. "Enter every night's totals in a spreadsheet," he said, "and make me a chart of the standings." Parker wanted the chart to look impressive, the kind you could point at like a lawyer on TV.

He typed the scores into a column, learned that the formula =SUM(B2:B8) would add the whole thing, and watched the total appear like magic. He picked a bar chart, and his heart sank. His bar looked tiny and Aunt Rosa's looked like a skyscraper. It made it seem like she had crushed them both, which wasn't true at all. The napkin said she was ahead by maybe four points out of nearly two hundred.

He leaned closer to the screen. Could the chart be lying, or was he reading it wrong? He noticed the little numbers running up the side of the chart, the value axis, and squinted at them. Instead of starting at zero, the axis started at 190. Parker sat back. The bars only showed the tips of the numbers, not the whole numbers. Was that why a small lead looked enormous? He had one simple idea for testing it. He double-clicked the axis and changed the starting value to zero.

The chart redrew itself instantly. All three bars shot up to nearly the same height, and the difference between Aunt Rosa and Grandpa became a sliver, a gradual slope of a gap rather than a cliff. Parker laughed out loud. "The chart isn't broken," he said to the empty kitchen. "The settings were just making it dramatic." He saved two versions, the honest one and the zoomed-in one, side by side.

He carried the laptop to the garage, where Grandpa was wrapping foam sleeves around the water pipes to insulate them before winter. Parker set the laptop on the workbench. "Aunt Rosa's ahead by four points," he said, "but watch what this chart does." He clicked from one version to the other, and the bars leaped apart, then drew close together.

Grandpa wiped his hands and studied the screen. "Same numbers, two different stories," he said.

"It's a little bit of a paradox," Parker said. "It looks like a huge win and a tiny win at the exact same time."

Grandpa grinned. "Which one do we show Rosa tonight?"

activity: to build a spreadsheet with a formula that adds a column and makes a bar chart
knowledge_domain: to build a spreadsheet with a formula that adds a column and makes a bar chart
fact: VisiCalc, written by Dan Bricklin and Bob Frankston and released for the Apple II in 1979, was the first spreadsheet program for personal computers.
story:
Chase slid into the seat next to the library's only working computer tower, the one with the sticky spacebar, and opened the spreadsheet program. His goal was simple: prove to his grandfather that Chase's dog-walking business had earned enough for the new bike. He typed his clients into column A and every payment into column B, then clicked the empty cell under the numbers.

"How do I make it add the whole column?" he asked, mostly to himself.

"Try the button that looks like a Greek E," said a voice. Marisol, the librarian, was reshelving books two feet away. "It evaluates everything you picked, but check the range, because if you grab the wrong cells it will cheerfully add the wrong numbers too."

Chase clicked it. A formula appeared in the cell, and the total showed 84 dollars. He blinked. That was wrong. He knew he had more than that, because eleven walks at ten dollars each was over a hundred, and there were extras. He leaned closer. The formula's little range only stretched partway down column B, stopping at row 8 when his list went to row 14. He couldn't see why at first, the computer had made its own choice silently, so he tested an idea: he dragged the corner of the range down to row 14 and watched the total jump to 132 dollars. The hidden cause was the range, not the math. "Ha," he said, quietly, because the library rules still applied even when you won.

"That's a spreadsheet," said Grandpa Joe, who had been reading a newspaper at the next table and now rolled his chair over. "You know I met one of those before you were born. VisiCalc, it was called. Dan Bricklin and Bob Frankston wrote it, and it came out for the Apple II in 1979. First spreadsheet program for personal computers, that one."

Chase turned. "You had a computer in 1979?"

"We couldn't afford one, so I stood in the store doing my tax sums on the display model until the manager made me buy something." Grandpa Joe smiled at the memory. "The machine was less volatile than my checkbook. One wrong subtraction and I'd panic. VisiCalc just recalculated."

Chase wanted the chart now, because a bar chart would convince Grandpa better than a number. He highlighted the client names and the payments, clicked the chart button, and got bars for everyone except Mrs. Okonkwo, whose two walks towered over everyone else's. Then he noticed something odd. The chart said Mrs. Okonkwo paid 40 dollars, but his notebook said she'd paid twice in one week because she'd tipped him. He'd logged the tip as a walk. He went back to the sheet, split the tip into its own column labeled "Tips," and made the chart again. Now the bars told the true story: steady walks, a small golden tower of extra tips, 132 total.

"Wait," Chase said, staring at the screen. "I didn't earn 132 for walks. I earned 112 in walks and 20 in tips." He had been about to show Grandpa a number that included tips as if they were guaranteed money, which meant next month's prediction would be wrong. He made a second chart with walks only, then a third with everything. Two charts. Truth and whole truth.

Grandpa Joe studied them for a long moment. "Which one's the bike money?"

"The walks one," Chase said. "Tips are volatile. The bike costs 199, so I need nine more walks, or seven if Mrs. Okonkwo keeps the tips coming." He thought about Mrs. Okonkwo's bad knee, how she always waved him off before he reached the porch steps so he wouldn't have to climb them, and he added a line to his sheet: "Pick up payment at mailbox, Mrs. O."

Marisol passed by again and dropped a stapled pile of beginner spreadsheet lessons on the desk. "The kid at table four was struggling with formulas too," she said. "You'll be the expert by Thursday."

"Table four?" Chase looked over. A smaller kid sat hunched in front of the other computer, jabbing at the keyboard with one finger. Chase saved his file, tucked the printouts of his charts under his arm, and walked over. "Hey," he said. "Want to see what happens when the range is too short?"

activity: to compare simple and compound interest on a savings account over five years
knowledge_domain: to compare simple and compound interest on a savings account over five years
fact: The simple interest formula is I = P x r x t: interest equals the principal times the yearly rate times the number of years.
story:
Grandpa's kitchen table had a sticky spot near the salt shaker, and Levi shifted his notebook away from it before he began. He had come for the weekend with one mission: figure out which savings account was better, because the ad from First River Bank was taped to his folder at home, and it made a big promise about interest.

"Grandpa, can I borrow your calculator?" he asked. Grandpa slid it across the table, then set down a glass of milk beside it without being asked, because he knew Levi always wanted milk when he was thinking.

Levi had copied the numbers from the ad. Two hundred dollars, five percent a year, five years. The ad called one option simple interest. Levi wrote the formula the bank's fine print gave, I equals P times r times t, and muttered it under his breath. "Interest equals the principal times the yearly rate times the number of years." Principal was the starting money, two hundred. Rate was five percent, which was point zero five. Time was five years. He multiplied: two hundred times point zero five was ten dollars a year, times five years was fifty dollars. Simple interest gave him fifty dollars.

But the ad also showed a second account, compound, with a bigger number at the end, and Levi didn't believe it. "Nobody gives away free money," he said. Grandpa only raised an eyebrow and went back to slicing an apple, laying the pieces on a plate where Levi could reach them.

Levi tested it the long way, year by year. With compound interest, the ten dollars from year one joined the two hundred, so year two earned interest on two hundred ten. He worked through all five years with the calculator, checking each step twice, and the final total came out higher than simple interest by a few dollars. Not magic, he realized, just the interest earning interest too. The difference was gradual at first, then wider, like a path that forks slowly and then heads for different hills. He drew two lines on a graph to portray it: one straight, one curving upward, crossing apart at year five.

"Grandpa, the compound one wins," Levi said, turning the notebook around. "But only if I leave the money alone the whole time." Grandpa looked at the graph, then at Levi, and pulled his own old bank book from a drawer.

"Fifty years," Grandpa said, tapping the balance. "Look what compound did for me."

activity: to read the rights listed in their country's constitution or charter and explain one in their own words
knowledge_domain: to read the rights listed in their country's constitution or charter and explain one in their own words
fact: The equality rights in section 15 of the Canadian Charter came into force in 1985, three years after the rest, to give governments time to update their laws.
story:
Camille spread the poster board across the kitchen table and weighed down the curling corners with mugs. The assignment was due Monday: pick one right from the Canadian Charter of Rights and Freedoms and explain it in your own words, out loud, to the class. She had chosen equality rights, mostly because it sounded impressive, and she had copied the exact words of section 15 onto an index card. Then she had flipped back to the schedule page at the front of the book to check the start date, and stopped. Every part of the Charter had come into force on the same day, except one.

"Mom, why does this page say section 15 came into force in 1985?" she asked, turning the book around. "The rest of it started three years before that. Did they print it wrong?"

Mom leaned over the table, still holding a dish towel. "That's what the page says."

Camille checked the school website, then the library database on her brother's old laptop. Both said the same thing. Equality rights, section 15, came into force in 1985, three years after the rest. She pushed the laptop away. "It's not a typo, then. Two sources can't make the same typo." Her first idea, that the date was a printing error, was refuted, and she felt oddly pleased about it. A wrong answer crossed off the list was still progress.

She sat with her chin on her fist and stared at the index card. What kind of right waits three years to start? Then an insight landed, small but solid: a law that makes everyone equal might need other laws changed first, because some old laws treated people differently. She couldn't see that directly, the way you can't see wind, only the branches moving. But she could test it. She wrote her idea on the back of the card: maybe the delay gave governments time to fix their laws so the equality rule wouldn't collide with them. It was a feasible explanation, simple enough to say out loud in one breath, and it fit every fact she had.

She practiced in front of the bathroom mirror, holding the card like a cue. "Equality rights are in section 15 of the Charter. They came into force in 1985, three years after the rest," she told her reflection, "and that extra time mattered, because a promise of equality has to be ready to work." Her voice wobbled on the last word, so she said it again, and the third time it came out steady.

At dinner she performed the whole thing for Mom and her little brother, who dropped spaghetti on the poster board twice. When she finished, Mom held up her water glass like a trophy. "To section 15," she said. "The right that waited." Camille laughed, pried the noodle off the poster, and picked up her marker to letter the title across the top.

activity: to read the rights listed in their country's constitution or charter and explain one in their own words
knowledge_domain: to read the rights listed in their country's constitution or charter and explain one in their own words
fact: Section 33 of the Canadian Charter, the notwithstanding clause, lets Parliament or a provincial legislature override certain rights for up to five years, and the override can be renewed.
story:
Simon's grandfather had taped the newspaper article to the fridge with three magnets, which meant he was serious. The headline said the provincial government was using Section 33 of the Canadian Charter, the notwithstanding clause, to override a right. At Sunday dinner, Grandpa and Simon's uncle argued about it until the lasagna went cold, and Simon sat there unable to follow any of it. That bugged him. So he made a plan: at Thursday's town hall meeting, where his class had to recite rights and explain one in their own words, he would figure out what that clause actually meant.

He started with the library copy of the Charter, copying rights onto index cards. Section 2, freedom of expression. Section 7, life, liberty and security. Section 15, equal protection. He practiced in the mirror, stumbled over "notwithstanding" six times, and wrote it out phonetically: not-with-stand-ing. His little sister quizzed him at breakfast. "That one's subjective," Simon said when she asked which right was the most important. "It depends who you ask. Grandpa says expression, Uncle Ray says equality."

Thursday night, the town hall smelled of coffee and floor wax. Simon's class sat in the front row. A boy named Marcus explained freedom of religion, and a girl explained voting rights. When Simon's turn came, his card stuck to his damp palm. He read Section 2 cleanly, then looked up at the crowd, and at Grandpa in the third row.

"Freedom of expression," Simon said, "means the government can't stop you from speaking your mind. But here's the part I didn't know two weeks ago. Section 33, the notwithstanding clause, lets Parliament or a provincial legislature override certain rights, but only for up to five years." He paused, testing his own idea. "So my question was, what's the point of a right if they can override it? I thought maybe the rights were fake. But five years isn't forever. And here's the thing I worked out: after five years, the override has to be renewed. That means somebody has to stand up in public and say, yes, we're doing it again. That part gets noticed."

Uncle Ray stood up in the back. "The kid's asking the right question."

"He's asking my question," Grandpa called out, "which is annoying, because I wanted to ask it."

The room laughed. Afterward, a woman from the school board asked Simon to write his explanation for the town newsletter, and asked him to disclose his sources, which meant showing which parts came from the Charter itself and which were his own idea. Simon spread his index cards across her table and tapped the one marked Section 33.

"This part's mine," he said. "The five years part is the Charter's. My grandpa taped the article to the fridge."

activity: to test whether a solution is an acid or a base using litmus paper and the pH scale
knowledge_domain: to test whether a solution is an acid or a base using litmus paper and the pH scale
fact: Most traditional bar soaps are basic, with a pH of around 9 to 10.
story:
Florence balanced three glasses on the kitchen counter: one with vinegar, one with water, and one with a fat pink bar of soap dissolving in warm water. Her science packet said litmus paper could tell an acid from a base, and Mrs. Okoye had promised the whole class would participate in the school science night, but only if they brought real results. Florence wanted the blue ribbon more than she had ever wanted anything, including the horse poster she'd saved up for last summer.

She tore a strip from her little booklet of translucent paper, so thin she could see the window light through it, and dipped it into the vinegar. The blue paper turned pink. "Acid," she said out loud, even though nobody was home yet. The plain tap water did nothing at all, which was strange until she remembered that the pH scale ran from zero to fourteen, and seven sat in the middle. Water was the middle. That meant each side had to be the opposite of the other, like a seesaw with seven as the balance point.

Then she dipped a fresh strip into the soapy water, and the paper turned a deep, determined blue. It had gone the opposite direction from the vinegar. Florence frowned. She had guessed soap was an acid, because it smelled sharp, and now her data sheet had a big fat wrong answer on it. She wrote "basic" in her neatest letters, then dug through the kitchen drawer until she found the strip of pH color chart Grandma had left from her canning days. Holding the paper against the squares, she saw it matched the box labeled 9. She tested it twice more, out of stubbornness, and it matched 9, then 10, then 9 again. So most regular soap bars weren't just barely basic; they were way up the scale, around 9 to 10, as far on the opposite side from vinegar as vinegar was from the middle.

Florence heard the door bang, and her little brother Theo skidded in, waving a paper. "Read this! Read this!" It was a note from his friend Marcus: "Dear Theo, I will trade you my robot eraser for your alloy ruler, the silver one that does not bend. Meet me at the bus stop tomorrow. Bring the ruler. P.S. does your sister know lava is an acid, tell her I said hi."

"Lava is not an acid," Florence said. "Also, don't trade that ruler, Grandpa got it from his machine shop." Theo, however, was staring at her colored papers like they were magic. "I want to participate in science night too," he announced. "I could be your assistant. I have a magnifying glass and everything." Florence looked at her data sheet, which needed exactly one more row filled in, and at Theo, who was already wearing the magnifying glass around his neck like a medal.

"You can record results," she said, sliding the notebook toward him. "Write 'soap, pH 9' right there." Theo picked up the pencil with tremendous ceremony, tongue between his teeth, and printed it in letters the size of his thumb. Then he dipped a fresh strip of litmus paper into the soapy water all by himself, held his breath, and watched it bloom blue. "It's going the wrong way for acid," he whispered. "It's going the other way, Flo. The total opposite way."
